svg.aria-label: Diagram: named locations, device filters and risk conditions in Microsoft Entra Conditional Access, showing how each signal is determined and how far it can be trusted, the device filter behaviour where a positive operator silently does not apply to an unregistered device, the fact that location is the proxy address re-evaluated about once an hour, and the split between real-time and offline risk detections
svg.title: Three signals that narrow a policy, and three different amounts of trust
svg.text: Three signals that narrow a policy — and none of them means quite what it says.
Where the user is, what they are on, and whether this looks wrong. Each is inferred, each has a latency, and one of them fails open.
What each signal actually is
SIGNAL
DERIVED FROM
HOW FAR TO TRUST IT
Network location
the public IP Entra sees
behind a proxy, that is the proxy’s address
Device filter
the device object in the directory
unregistered device → every property is null
Risk
ID Protection detections
mostly offline — the sign-in already happened
The device filter case that fails open
“For a device that is unregistered with Microsoft Entra ID, all device properties are considered as null values.” So:
device.extensionAttribute1 -eq "SAW"
A positive operator. On an unregistered device the
filter does not apply at all — so an exclude-mode
block policy never blocks the unmanaged laptop.
device.extensionAttribute1 -ne "SAW"
A negative operator. This one does apply to an
unregistered device. “The best way to target policies
for unregistered devices is by using the negative operator.”
And a quieter one: extensionAttributes1-15 only carry a value at evaluation time if the device is “Microsoft Intune managed,
compliant, or Microsoft Entra hybrid joined”. Tag a device in Graph and forget that, and the tag is invisible to the policy.
Location is the proxy, and it is checked hourly
“The X-Forwarded-For (XFF) header, which contains the
user’s public IP address, isn’t used because there’s no
validation that it comes from a trusted source.”
Keeping a proxy or VPN egress list current is
“nearly impossible” — so prefer a device control.
Re-evaluated on token refresh: “By default, this check
occurs once an hour.” Leaving the corporate network
is noticed within the hour, not at the door.
Limits: 195 named locations, 2000 ranges each.
Risk arrives late, and mostly after the fact
Real-time, so it can block the sign-in itself:
anonymous IP, unfamiliar sign-in properties, verified
threat actor IP, suspicious MFA approval.
Offline — the sign-in has already completed:
atypical travel, impossible travel, malicious IP,
suspicious browser, token issuer anomaly, leaked
credentials, and most of the rest.
Without P2 you get “Additional risk detected” and
no detail at all — a signal you cannot act on.
Two detections worth reading twice
Password spray fires only on success.
“Unsuccessful spray attempts against your users don’t
generate a detection.” If you see one, “the attacker achieved a successful credential validation against a user in your tenant”.
Leaked credentials is always high.
Microsoft validates the found credential “against your tenant’s
current valid password hashes” and fires only on a match — “verified credential exposure, not a heuristic signal”. Compare
anomalous token, where “there’s still a higher than normal chance” of false positives at low and medium risk.
And the assignment that silently covers less than it reads: “Conditional Access policies support built-in roles. Conditional Access
policies are not enforced for other role types including administrative unit-scoped or custom roles.”
Sources: Network assignment in Conditional Access, Filter for devices, and What are risk detections?, on Microsoft Learn.
